patient_information: A 28-year-old West African man from Ghana, who is short for an adult. He has a history of a previous ulcer on his right ankle some years ago which took about a year to heal.
chief_complaint: A painful ulcer on his left ankle that has been present for the past 4 months and is not healing.
history_of_present_illness: For the past four months, the patient has had a painful, non-healing ulcer on his left ankle. There was no history of prior trauma. He also complains of pain in his right thigh and in both knees. He had a similar ulcer on his right ankle years ago which took a year to resolve.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from West Africa and presented to a clinic in Ghana. He is self-employed.
vitals: Temperature was 36.6°C, pulse was 88 bpm, and blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg.
physical_exam: The patient is short, pale, and has a tinge of jaundice. There is an ulcer on his left ankle next to the medial malleolus, with surrounding hyperpigmented skin. Tenderness was noted in both knee joints and in his right thigh. The rest of the physical examination was normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial laboratory results showed a high white blood cell count of 17.6 x10^9/L, haemoglobin of 6.9 g/dL, and a fasting blood glucose of 4.8 mmol/L. The peripheral blood film showed irreversibly sickled cells, polychromasia, target cells, and nucleated red cells. A sickling test was positive, and haemoglobin electrophoresis confirmed a homozygous HbSS-type. A wound swab grew Pseudomonas species sensitive to levofloxacin. Radiography of the left leg showed a periosteal reaction with slightly sclerotic bones. At a 6-year follow-up, his WBC was 9.2 x10^9/L and his haemoglobin had increased to 8.3 g/dL.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnosis included venous ulcer, due to the chronic nature and site. Various hereditary haemolytic anaemias complicated by leg ulcers were considered, such as thalassaemia, spherocytosis, and pyruvate kinase deficiency, with sickle cell disease being the most likely in the West African context given the bone pain, jaundice, and pallor. Other possibilities included tropical ulcer, diabetic ulcer, chronic osteomyelitis with a discharging sinus, Buruli ulcer, other mycobacterial infections, pyoderma gangrenosum, and malignant diseases.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was diagnosed with sickle cell disease with a chronic ankle ulcer. Management included alternate daily wound dressing with normal saline irrigation and povidone-iodine, systemic antibiotics for the Pseudomonas infection, and daily folic acid supplementation. His recurrent bone pain was managed with hydration, prompt treatment of infections, paracetamol, and tramadol. Strict bed rest was difficult to enforce as he was self-employed. On follow-up 3 years later, the ulcer was still not healed, and skin grafting was under consideration. Six years later, the wound remained unhealed, and he was receiving dressing changes three times a week.
final_diagnosis: The diagnosis was sickle cell disease with a chronic ankle ulcer. This was established based on the clinical presentation of a chronic, non-healing ulcer, bone pains, pallor, and jaundice in a young West African man. The diagnosis was definitively confirmed by laboratory tests, including a peripheral blood film showing sickled red cells, a positive sickling test, and haemoglobin electrophoresis which revealed a homozygous HbSS-type.
